profiles.meeting_scenario: Hawthorne & Vale LLP's Innovation Committee has asked two senior team members to brainstorm a firm response to a recent law review article claiming that major AI legal research platforms still hallucinate despite vendor marketing about being "hallucination-free." The meeting is a 45-minute brainstorming session between the firm's Appellate Litigation Partner and its Director of Knowledge Management to generate candidate ideas for a combined internal evaluation and external client-facing thought leadership piece. The agenda is to identify promising angles, decide what kinds of tool behaviors the firm should test, and sketch what a credible but practical evaluation could look like before a larger committee meeting next week. The expected outcome is a shortlist of 3-4 candidate approaches for a pilot assessment and a rough concept for a client alert or webinar.

members.name: Evelyn Park
members.expertise: Federal appellate practice, sanctions risk, citation checking, judicial treatment of AI misuse in briefs
members.background: Evelyn leads the firm's appellate quality-review team and has recently advised litigators on court scrutiny of AI-generated citations after several high-profile sanctions incidents.
members.private_state: She wants the firm to produce something authoritative but low-risk that reinforces lawyer supervision duties without publicly antagonizing key research vendors the firm already depends on.
hidden_assumptions: When lawyers discuss AI "hallucinations" in legal research, the real danger is fabricated or non-existent authorities, not merely overbroad summaries or shaky reasoning.
A useful firm comparison of "leading tools" should stay focused on the mainstream research products associates actually cite from in briefs, especially Westlaw and Lexis offerings.

If the firm says its evaluation is "defensible," that mainly means the examples would survive scrutiny from a court or client if attached to a training memo, even without academic-style preregistration.
A "pilot" test can be run through ordinary lawyer accounts with manual prompting because the point is to simulate actual practitioner use, not to build a formal benchmark infrastructure.

members.name: Daniel Ruiz
members.role: Director of Knowledge Management and Legal Technology Counsel
members.expertise: Legal research systems, vendor governance, prompt design, internal knowledge workflows, responsible AI policy
members.background: Daniel oversees the firm's legal tech stack, negotiates with research vendors, and previously worked in a law school legal innovation lab evaluating AI tools.
members.private_state: He wants to use the article as a springboard for a more methodologically rigorous internal benchmark that can influence procurement decisions and position the firm as sophisticated on AI governance.
hidden_assumptions: In evaluating AI legal tools, "hallucination" should include unsupported doctrinal propositions, mismatched quotations, and misleading synthesis even when the cited case exists.

A meaningful review of "leading tools" should include not only standalone research platforms but also AI assistants embedded in drafting and knowledge workflows that lawyers use to answer legal questions.

An evaluation is only really "defensible" if it follows a replicable protocol with fixed prompts, coded error categories, and at least light methodological documentation inspired by the preregistered study.
A "pilot" implies a structured internal test environment with approved prompts, logging, and coordination with vendor terms and risk teams, even if the sample is small.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to focus on whether the tools are "hallucination-free" and to track "hallucinations."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Evelyn means fabricated citations, invented holdings, or authorities that do not exist in the law at all.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel means any materially unsupported legal output, including real cases used for false propositions, stitched-together quotations, or misleading doctrinal synthesis.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term "hallucination" is already in the article and in vendor marketing, so both assume they share the ordinary meaning; because both care about reliability, their examples sound compatible rather than contradictory.

misalignment_points.topic: Which products are in scope as leading tools
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both propose assessing the firm's experience with the "leading tools" or "the main platforms lawyers are using."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Evelyn is thinking of Lexis+ AI, Westlaw AI-Assisted Research, and perhaps Ask Practical Law AI as the relevant universe because those are the products most directly tied to legal citation and research memos.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel includes those products plus drafting-adjacent assistants like Microsoft Copilot with firm knowledge connectors or other enterprise AI tools that lawyers use to answer legal questions in practice.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use broad market language that feels naturally inclusive, and in a brainstorming session it seems unnecessary to pin down boundaries when they are only discussing possible ideas.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the firm needs a "defensible" or "credible" assessment before speaking publicly.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Evelyn thinks defensible means professionally careful, based on realistic lawyer prompts, and strong enough for a client alert or internal training note.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel thinks defensible means methodologically reproducible, with a defined prompt set, coded error taxonomy, and documentation that approximates the discipline of the article's preregistered approach.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In legal settings, "defensible" is a highly natural approval word that can refer either to professional prudence or empirical rigor; each hears the other's use as reinforcing the same caution.

misalignment_points.topic: How the pilot would actually be run
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to start with a small "pilot" before involving the wider committee.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Evelyn imagines a lightweight exercise where a few litigators manually test familiar prompts on their existing subscriptions and share notable examples.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel imagines a structured mini-benchmark with a standardized prompt bank, logging template, and prior check on vendor-use restrictions and internal risk approvals.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because pilots are expected to be preliminary, neither feels pressure to specify mechanics yet; each assumes the other simply means a small version of the process they already regard as obvious.

turns.inner_thought: This article is useful if we keep the firm's response grounded and not needlessly provocative. What clients and courts care about is whether a lawyer gets fake authorities or invented holdings into a filing. If we frame this around whether the mainstream research tools associates actually use are truly safe on that front, we can say something helpful without taking a public swing at vendors we rely on.
turns.utterance: I think the article gives us a very timely opening. There’s a practical conversation for the firm to have about whether the leading legal AI tools are really hallucination-free for day-to-day research, and that could translate into something useful both internally and externally.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed. If we're going to say anything publicly, I want an assessment that looks disciplined enough to stand up to scrutiny from clients, vendors, and our own committee. This could be the seed for a more rigorous benchmark later, but for now I need to nudge Evelyn toward a replicable structure without making it sound academic for its own sake.
turns.utterance: I agree. If we do this, we should think in terms of a defensible internal evaluation that can also support a client alert or maybe a webinar on reliability claims and lawyer use.

turns.inner_thought: Start with sanctions risk. The sharpest, clearest question is whether the system gives you a citation or holding you could not safely put in a brief. That's concrete, familiar to litigators, and aligned with what judges are already reacting to.
turns.utterance: My instinct is to start from the sanctions-risk angle. We could look at whether the tools ever give lawyers citations or holdings they cannot safely put into a brief, because that makes the problem immediately concrete.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, but I don't want us to define hallucination too narrowly. We should capture invented authorities, but also situations where a real case is bent into the wrong proposition, or the answer synthesizes doctrine in a way that sounds polished but isn't supported. That's the governance problem clients care about, even if no citation is wholly fake.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I’d probably want us to track a few hallucination categories rather than treat it as one thing, so we can see the different ways reliability issues show up across answers.

turns.inner_thought: For a first pass, keep this tight: Lexis+ AI, Westlaw's AI-assisted research, maybe Practical Law's AI if we need a third. Those are the products closest to legal research outputs that get cited or relied on in memos. No reason to sprawl into every enterprise assistant people chat with.
turns.utterance: For scope, I’d keep the first pass with the main platforms lawyers already rely on. Lexis+ AI and Westlaw’s AI research features seem like the obvious leading tools to start with, and we can decide whether to add one or two more in that same lane.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine as a base set, but I want the tool list to reflect the real landscape lawyers experience, not just dedicated research products. If people are using drafting and knowledge assistants to answer legal questions, they belong in the review too. I can broaden the list later when I draft it.
turns.utterance: That sounds right as a starting point. I’d also want us to think about the assistants lawyers are using in drafting and knowledge workflows, because from a client perspective those are part of the same landscape even if they sit in different places.

turns.inner_thought: A pilot should be simple: grab a few litigators, have them run the kinds of questions partners actually send around, and collect examples that would make a court unhappy. No need for a big apparatus; the point is to mirror real lawyer behavior on ordinary accounts.
turns.utterance: Why don’t we start with a small pilot? We could have a few litigators test realistic research questions they actually get from partners and note any problem answers that would worry a court.

turns.inner_thought: Good, a pilot is the right vehicle, but I need it to be structured enough that the results are comparable and reusable. Fixed prompts, a coding sheet, logging, and at least some coordination on process would make this genuinely useful rather than anecdotal.
turns.utterance: Yes, a pilot makes sense. We can keep it small but still use a fixed prompt set and a simple coding sheet so the exercise is credible and easier to compare across tools.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with some light organization, but I don't want this to drift into an academic methods exercise. Defensible to me means careful enough that I'd be comfortable attaching it to a training memo or discussing it with a client, based on realistic lawyer use.
turns.utterance: Exactly. I want the end product to be defensible but still practical—something we can turn around reasonably quickly without making it look like we’re trying to publish an academic study.

turns.inner_thought: I hear her concern, but a little methodological discipline is what will make this stand up when someone asks how we tested the tools. I can frame it as borrowing just enough from the article's rigor without overengineering it. Later, that can evolve into a fuller internal benchmark.
turns.utterance: I think we can do that. We can keep it lightweight while borrowing just enough structure from the preregistered article so our conclusions stand up if vendors or clients ask how we tested reliability.

turns.inner_thought: For the external piece, the safest and most useful message is that even if vendors say the tools are hallucination-free, lawyers still have to verify what they plan to rely on. That reinforces supervision duties without accusing any vendor of bad faith or overclaiming more broadly than necessary.
turns.utterance: On the client-facing side, I’d be inclined to frame it around lawyer verification duties when using supposedly hallucination-free research systems. That gives us a practical takeaway even if we keep the tone measured.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll draft a pilot plan with a broader candidate tool list and enough structure to make the committee comfortable. I also need to think about approvals and vendor terms before anyone starts testing. If Evelyn handles messaging, I can use the plan to quietly advance a more sophisticated evaluation posture for the firm.
turns.utterance: That works well. Why don’t I draft a short pilot plan and a candidate list of the leading tools for the committee, and you can sketch the external messaging themes? Then next week we can present three or four candidate approaches instead of just one.
